title: Antimicrobial Allergy Assessment and Penicillin De-Labelling Referral
specialty: Allergy and Immunology / Infectious Diseases / Primary Care

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults and children with a recorded or suspected antibiotic allergy, mainly penicillin: history-based phenotype, documentation, acute reaction handling, risk stratification for de-labelling, direct oral challenge by trained non-allergists in hospital, and referral. Uses NICE CG183, the British Society for Allergy and Clinical Immunology (BSACI) 2022 de-labelling guideline (via a published review) and the Saudi Ministry of Health (MOH) anaphylaxis protocol.
findings: Rebuilt from the thin 21 Oct 2026 version: reaction phenotypes with timing, low-risk and high-risk criteria, the oral challenge protocol, documentation requirements and six management steps added.
Medicine plan stays 'no drug indicated': the challenge medicine is a test dose given by a trained de-labelling team, and acute anaphylaxis treatment sits in the anaphylaxis topic.
All thresholds trace to sources opened on 22 Oct 2026.
unverifiedSections: The BSACI 2022 full text was not opened; low-risk/high-risk boxes and the challenge protocol come from a peer-reviewed summary (Tipton and Marikar 2025). The summary gives no milligram doses for the challenge; doses follow the BNF or BNFC and local protocol.
No Saudi national guideline on penicillin de-labelling was found; the Saudi MOH anaphylaxis protocol is cited for acute reactions only.
Normal values for skin and challenge tests are descriptive; testing reagents and interpretation are specialist decisions.
Distinguishing features for differentials are clinical descriptions not taken from an opened guideline section.

pathophysiology.summary: Immediate reactions, usually within 1 hour, are mediated by mast cells and include urticaria, angioedema and anaphylaxis (NICE CG183, Section 1.1). Non-immediate reactions are T-cell mediated: benign rashes appear 6–10 days after first exposure or within 3 days of re-exposure (NICE CG183, Section 1.1). Severe cutaneous reactions — drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) at 2–6 weeks, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) or toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) at 7–14 days — involve organs (NICE CG183, Section 1.1). About 95% of penicillin labels are wrong on testing (Tipton 2025).
keyMechanisms: Immediate (under 1 hour): anaphylaxis, urticaria, angioedema (NICE CG183, Section 1.1).
Non-immediate, no systemic involvement: maculopapular rash or fixed drug eruption, 6–10 days after first exposure or within 3 days of re-exposure (NICE CG183, Section 1.1).
DRESS at 2–6 weeks; SJS/TEN at 7–14 days; acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis at 3–5 days (NICE CG183, Section 1.1).
5.9% of people carry a penicillin label; 95% are not allergic on testing (Tipton 2025).
Fewer than 7% of children react on re-exposure (Tipton 2025).

symptoms: Itchy rash or hives during or soon after the drug (NICE CG183, Section 1.1).
Lip, face or tongue swelling (NICE CG183, Section 1.1).
Gastrointestinal upset only — makes allergy less likely (NICE CG183, Section 1.1).
physicalSigns: Widespread red macules or papules (NICE CG183, Section 1.1).
Blisters, skin peeling, mucosal involvement or purpura — severe phenotype (Tipton 2025, Box 3).
Hypotension or bronchospasm with skin signs — anaphylaxis (NICE CG183, Section 1.1).
redFlags: Anaphylaxis: airway, breathing or circulation problem, usually with skin changes (Saudi MOH anaphylaxis protocol, p. 1).
Mucosal ulceration, blistering or skin detachment — SJS/TEN (NICE CG183, Section 1.1).
Fever, rash and organ involvement 2–6 weeks after starting — DRESS (NICE CG183, Section 1.1).
Hepatitis, nephritis or vasculitis with a drug (NICE CG183, Section 1.1).
precipitants: non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) in asthma with nasal polyps (NICE CG183, Section 1.4).
Childhood rash during a viral illness treated with amoxicillin — a common low-risk label (Tipton 2025, Box 2).
Family history alone — not a reason to label (Tipton 2025, Box 2).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Rash with an infection in childhood and no other features; low-risk history (Tipton 2025, Box 2).
Gastrointestinal upset or thrush only; makes allergy less likely (NICE CG183, Section 1.1).
Another cause present, for example infection or food (NICE CG183, Section 1.1).
Blistering, mucosal or organ involvement; never challenge — refer (NICE CG183, Section 1.4).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Reaction during or after the drug, the drug is known to cause it, or a similar reaction before (NICE CG183, Section 1.1).

Gastrointestinal upset, thrush, family history only, penicillin tolerated since, benign rash starting more than 1 hour after the first dose, or a childhood rash with no other history (Tipton 2025, Box 2).

Rash within 1 hour, lasting over 24 hours or covering over 10% of the body; blisters, mucosal involvement or purpura; adrenaline or hospital treatment needed; severe asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD); severe aortic stenosis; acute illness; pregnancy (Tipton 2025, Box 3).
Suspected anaphylaxis or a severe non-immediate skin reaction (DRESS, SJS, TEN) (NICE CG183, Section 1.4).

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Record drug, reaction, severity, date, timing, doses before onset and route (NICE CG183, Section 1.2).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat an acute reaction
actions: Anaphylaxis: intramuscular adrenaline per the Saudi MOH protocol (adult 0.3–0.5 mg) and the anaphylaxis topic (Saudi MOH anaphylaxis protocol, p. 1).
Take timed tryptase samples (NICE anaphylaxis, Recommendation 1.1.4).

clinicalManagement.title: Take the allergy history
actions: Separate immediate, non-immediate and severe cutaneous phenotypes (NICE CG183, Section 1.1).
Record drug, brand, dose, route, indication, reaction, timing and drugs to avoid (NICE CG183, Section 1.2).
Record status as 'drug allergy', 'none known' or 'unable to ascertain' (NICE CG183, Section 1.2).

clinicalManagement.title: Stratify risk
actions: Apply the BSACI low-risk and high-risk criteria (see Diagnostic criteria) (Tipton 2025, Boxes 2–3).
Low risk: offer direct oral challenge by the trained de-labelling team.
High risk: refer to specialist allergy services; no challenge outside them.

clinicalManagement.title: Direct oral challenge
actions: Written consent; observations before and after each dose (Tipton 2025, Box 4).
Single full dose or graded 10% → 50% → remainder, 30 minutes apart; observe 1 hour after the last dose (Tipton 2025, Box 4).
Dose by age and weight using the BNF or BNFC (Tipton 2025, Box 4).

clinicalManagement.title: Refer when needed
actions: After suspected anaphylaxis or DRESS, SJS or TEN (NICE CG183, Section 1.4).
When a beta-lactam is the only effective treatment or will be needed often; consider if beta-lactams and one other class cannot be used (NICE CG183, Section 1.4).

clinicalManagement.title: Close the loop
actions: Negative challenge: remove the label, tell the patient in writing and inform the general practitioner (Tipton 2025, Box 4).
Give written instructions on delayed symptoms after discharge (Tipton 2025, Box 4).
If allergy confirmed: record the drugs and classes to avoid and safe alternatives (NICE CG183, Section 1.3).

medicationPlan.note: No treatment medicine belongs to this assessment pathway. The challenge dose is a test given by a trained team using the BNF or BNFC and local protocol. Acute anaphylaxis treatment follows the Saudi MOH anaphylaxis protocol (see the anaphylaxis and upper-airway topics). For endocarditis prophylaxis, ESC 2023 advises not to use cephalosporins after anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria with penicillin or ampicillin (ESC 2023, Table 6 footnote).

guidelineComparison.title: Who may be tested outside an allergy clinic

values: Refer to specialist services when a beta-lactam is essential or often needed
Low-risk patients can be de-labelled by trained non-allergists in hospital
Specialist investigations; no IgE testing outside specialists

guidelineComparison.note: The two sources differ in setting; neither is merged.

learningObjectives: Classify a reported reaction by phenotype and timing.
Document allergy status to NICE CG183 standard.
keyPoints: Gastrointestinal upset alone is not allergy.
Never challenge after SJS, TEN or DRESS.
pitfalls: Leaving a low-risk label in place and using broader antibiotics.
Using an IgE blood test to diagnose allergy in primary care.
Removing the label without telling the patient and general practitioner.

patientEducation: Explain the result and which drugs are safe or must be avoided (NICE CG183, Section 1.3).
Carry allergy information and share it at every healthcare contact (NICE CG183, Section 1.3).
Check with a pharmacist before buying over-the-counter medicines (NICE CG183, Section 1.3).
lifestyleAndDiet: No dietary measure applies; avoid only the confirmed drugs or classes.
dischargeCriteria: Allergy record updated with phenotype and drugs to avoid.
Written information given; referral sent where criteria met.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Reconcile the allergy record after the specialist or challenge result and at every transfer of care (NICE CG183, Section 1.2).
